name: Meridian Munitions Snapper-22 'Cricket'
description:
The Meridian Munitions Snapper-22 is an eight-shot double-action revolver chambered in .22 LR, built with a lightweight aluminum frame and a three-inch barrel. It is the cheapest revolver Meridian Munitions produces — cheaper even than the Roundhouse — and fills the absolute bottom of the revolver market. The small caliber allows eight rounds in a compact cylinder, giving the Cricket more capacity than most revolvers twice its price.

The Cricket is not a weapon anyone chooses if they have other options. The .22 LR round from a three-inch barrel is marginal for self-defense by any standard, and the aluminum frame feels insubstantial in hand. But the weapon is nearly silent compared to larger calibers, produces virtually no recoil, and costs so little that losing or discarding it carries no financial consequence. These characteristics have made it unexpectedly popular among populations who need a weapon that won't draw attention.

In Shelf districts, the Cricket occupies a specific niche: it is the weapon people carry when they don't want anyone to know they're carrying a weapon. The mild report won't echo through apartment corridors, the small frame disappears in a coat pocket, and the .22 LR round — while weak — is still lethal at the distances that matter in hallways and stairwells.
specifications:
caliber: .22 LR
effective_range: 10 meters
rate_of_fire: Double-action revolver
magazine_capacity: 8 rounds (cylinder)
weight: 0.28 kg
tactical_use: A minimal-capability deep-concealment revolver. The .22 LR round is insufficient against any form of body armor and marginal against unarmored targets. The eight-round capacity provides more opportunities to land a decisive hit than the caliber might otherwise allow. The weapon's primary tactical value is concealability and discretion — it is very quiet and very small.
cultural_context: The Cricket is the weapon of people who can't afford to be seen carrying a weapon. Its very existence is a commentary on the layers of vulnerability in GLMZ — there are people for whom even the act of being armed is dangerous, and the Cricket is designed for them.
known_users: Elderly residents who cannot manage recoil
Couriers carrying contraband who need plausible deniability
story_hooks: A witness protection subject is given a Cricket as their only defense — eight rounds of .22 LR against professional killers. The weapon's inadequacy is the point: if the situation reaches the Cricket, the protection has already failed.
A string of murders in a residential block are committed with .22 LR — the rounds are so quiet that neighbors don't hear the shots, and the weapon is never found because it's worth less than a meal.

physical_description.visual_profile: A diminutive, almost toy-like revolver with a stubby profile. The compact cylinder dominates the frame, giving it a squat, beetle-backed appearance. Despite its small stature, it maintains classic revolver proportions—nothing looks obviously broken or jury-rigged, just... intentionally minimal.
physical_description.dimensions: Overall length 16.5 cm, cylinder diameter 3.2 cm, barrel length 7.6 cm, grip height 8.9 cm
physical_description.weight_description: Feather-light and insubstantial in hand—the aluminum frame delivers almost no tactile reassurance. It feels like holding a dense plastic toy rather than a serious firearm. The lightness is both its strength (unnoticed in a pocket) and its weakness (no momentum, no heft).
physical_description.primary_material: Anodized aluminum frame, blued steel cylinder and barrel
physical_description.finish: Matte charcoal anodize on the frame with micro-texture to prevent slipping; deep blue steel cylinder showing light wear at the charge holes from repeated loading; barrel in matching blued steel with light muzzle damage from cheap ammunition
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal gray frame with navy blue cylinder and barrel; minimal accent colors—just the small silver-plated cylinder latch and trigger guard
physical_description.grip_texture: Cheap rubberized polymer panels, slightly tacky and scored with fine crosshatching. The grip is thin and angular—ergonomics were sacrificed for weight and cost
distinctive_features: Eight-round cylinder (more than typical compact revolvers) with deep, slightly rough charge holes
Minimalist trigger guard—barely protruding, almost recessed into the frame
Three-inch barrel with visible tool marks from mass production
Tiny ejector rod barely longer than the cylinder
No rails, no ports, no optic mounts—absolutely stripped of anything superfluous
Faint tooling marks and parting lines visible in the aluminum—signs of investment casting rather than precision machining
Hammer spur worn smooth from cheap holster draws
Cylinder release button sits flush with the frame
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: "MERIDIAN MUNITIONS" stamped in small serif font along the left side of the barrel, barely legible under dull lighting. Serial number stamped into the frame under the cylinder crane, partially obscured by anodize. No other branding—the Cricket eschews aesthetic pretense.
physical_description.condition_typical: Worn but functional. The aluminum frame shows light oxidation under the anodize, the barrel's bluing is worn to pale gray at the muzzle and around the front sight post, and the grip panels are scratched and dulled. Cylinder shows carbon fouling around the charge holes. The weapon functions perfectly but looks like it has been carried, lost, found, and carried again.
